Fuel cells · Commercial / expanding

Solid oxide fuel cell · SOFC

Oxide ions formed at the air electrode move to the fuel electrode and react with fuel. Electrons flow through the external circuit.

Animated operating principles

Ion and electron pathways

O²⁻ · electrolyte / membrane Electrons e⁻ · external circuit

Simplified reaction directions and pathways. Actual particle numbers and speeds differ.

Electrode and electrolyte principles

Oxide ions O²⁻ pass through a high-temperature ceramic electrolyte.

Air electrode: ½O₂ + 2e⁻ → O²⁻ / Fuel electrode: H₂ + O²⁻ → H₂O + 2e⁻

Advantages

High electrical efficiency, combined heat and power, and fuel flexibility

Drawbacks & challenges

High-temperature maintenance, slow startup and thermal-cycle durability

Materials & supply constraints

Ceramics, nickel and other materials vary by design; platinum is not always needed.

Main applications

Buildings, data centers and distributed generation

SOFC high-temperature operation and heat use

Solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) use a ceramic electrolyte that conducts oxygen ions at high temperatures. High-temperature operation can support fuel processing and useful high-grade heat, but it also creates thermal management and material degradation challenges.

Can SOFC use fuels other than hydrogen?

Depending on system design, natural gas and other fuels may be reformed for use. Reforming equipment, fuel contaminants, carbon deposition and emissions still need evaluation.

Why are frequent starts and stops challenging?

Repeated heating and cooling can stress high-temperature components. Start-up time, duty cycle, availability and maintenance plans therefore matter in practical projects.
